claims_disputed.claim: DeepRepoQA outperforms state-of-the-art ReAct-style agents on all backbones (largest gain 7.08 over SWE-agent on Qwen3-Coder)
claims_disputed.reason: Table 2 margins over the best agent per backbone are +0.88, +3.41, +2.10 and +4.67. They come from one run per cell with MCTS exploration at temperature 0.7, on the authors' own benchmark and rubric. App. C.4 reports a human-vs-LLM system-ranking Spearman of only 0.900 over 6 systems, so the two panels order at least one pair differently. That human check covers only GPT-5.1 answers, where SWE-agent and OpenHands sit 1.17 apart. Sub-5-point gaps are therefore not resolved by this judge, and 'outperforms on all backbones' is a point-estimate statement.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: AST name lookups (FindClass/FindFunction/FindCodeSnippet with file_pattern) are core actions of the proposed system (§3.1-3.2, Table 1), and the lexical-only arm keeps 63.36 of 64.43 (Table 3). The paper uses and relies on the pattern without isolating it against a semantic-only arm, which is 'introduces', not 'neutral'.

missed_issues: Direct prompting with no repository access already scores 50-52/100 (Table 2), and Relevance and Clarity sit at about 13-17/20 for every method including Direct. About half the 0-100 scale therefore rewards fluent generic text, and the effective spread is mostly Correctness, Completeness and Reasoning. Clarity has Krippendorff alpha 0.32-0.41 (Table C1).

The three human experts in App. C are not identified (affiliation, independence from the authors, blinding to system identity are not stated), although the benchmark, rubric and judge prompt are the authors' own.

The App. E.3 success patterns (100% of answers scoring >=73 reached the correct file within two hops; 80% used symbol-anchored lookups; ViewCode before Finish 'strongly correlated' with Correctness) come from manual inspection of selected trajectories with no denominators or test. They are outcome-selected correlations, not evidence that adding these steps raises accuracy.

Uncontrolled conflict with sibling 2608.01507 on the same SWE-QA question set: there, a ReAct agent with vector search beat a grep-plus-subagent agent on every model, while here removing SemanticSearch from the agent costs only 1.07 points. Both agree that agentic exploration beats one-shot RAG but disagree on how much embeddings matter inside the agent, and the paper does not discuss it.

Against the better RAG baseline, the plain ReAct agent OpenHands gains only +1.2 (Qwen3-Coder) and +1.4 (GPT-5.1), versus +7-8 on GLM-4.6 and Kimi K2 (Table 2). The agent-over-RAG advantage is backbone-dependent and much of DeepRepoQA's edge on strong coders comes from its evaluation step (Table 3: -3.50 without it).
note: I agree with the review's scores (my relevance is 3 rather than 4 because nothing tests cross-repo questions or Spring wiring), its verdict, and most stances, including P43 'supports' for exploration agents over one-shot embedding RAG. I lower the headline 'outperforms ReAct agents on all backbones' from moderate to weak. The margins are single-run point estimates below the resolution of the judge panel, which the paper's own App. C.4 ranking agreement (rho 0.900) exposes. I upgrade P05 from neutral to introduces because AST symbol lookup is a core, relied-upon component, even though it is not isolated. The review was not too harsh anywhere: the efficiency and judge-reliability claims are fairly graded moderate. What survives is the agent-over-RAG gap, about 10-14 points on the 30-question Java subset and 3.3-10.7 points for DeepRepoQA over the better RAG in Python, plus qualitative failure modes the team can turn into checks.
